Cheaper Volkswagen ID. Cross Is Now Available With a 37 kWh Battery Pack; This Is How Much It Costs
6 photos
Photo: Volkswagen AG
Volkswagen continues to democratize its electrified and all-electric range, introduces a more affordable version of the ID. Cross with a smaller 37-kWh pack at home in Germany, starting from €27,995, which is the equivalent of a little over $31k at the current exchange rate.
The German automaker is in deep trouble – we all know that. But the company has actually timed its soft EV reboot quite well, as the Old Continent is increasingly leaning toward EV models as an alternative to escape the high oil prices of recent months. The only problem is that the Chinese are also here to try and take advantage of the new status quo.
Volkswagen is ready to open a new chapter in its EV book, though, and has already revealed the all-new or refreshed VW ID.3 Neo, ID. Polo, ID. Polo GTI, ID. Cross, plus the newly unveiled ID. Tiguan . The latter is trying to make us forget about the rather appalling and boring ID.4 with a family-oriented proposal, but the Old Continent will also take a look at the ID. Cross, which is smaller and nimbler across town.
Anyway, to make it even more enticing, Volkswagen is now starting pre-sales for the new ID. Cross with a smaller 37-kWh battery pack. The electric subcompact crossover SUV, which is basically the EV equivalent of the VW T-Cross model, has two battery options for the powertrain: 37-kWh LFP or 52-kWh NMC battery.
The smaller version “is primarily aimed at customers who mainly drive in urban traffic and on typical commuting routes and at the same time value an attractive entry-level price” summarizes VW's offer, as pricing for the Trend model at home in Germany kicks off at less than €28k. The smallest battery pack is available with the 85 kW (116 ps or 114 hp) and 99 kW (135 ps or 133 hp) drive systems, as well as the Trend, Life, and Style equipment lines.
Initially, only the larger 52 kWh battery pack was available to order, but now the lower purchase and operating costs model is also up for grabs, announced with a WLTP range of up to 324 km (201 miles) and a DC rapid charging system, allowing a recharge from 10 to 80 per cent in around 23 minutes, as standard. It can even drive on highways, as the top speed is 160 kph or 99 mph.
Right off the bat, the entry-level Trend version comes with standard perks like front and rear Park Distance Control and smartphone integration via “App Connect”, while Life and Style equipment lines bring comfort and technology features from higher classes like “Connected Travel Assist” or a Harman Kardon sound system, among others. Hyundai Unveils i30 Sedan N Monochrome Because Customers Wanted a Toned-Down Look
16 photos
Photo: Hyundai
Hyundai has officially unveiled the Hyundai i30 Sedan N Monochrome. The special limited-edition version of the performance sedan moves away from the vibrant trim accents, going instead for a dark, minimalist, and stripped-back look. Only 200 lucky customers will be able to get their hands on the stealthy Hyundai sedan.
Understated yet undeniable. This is how Hyundai makes a long story short with the all-new i30 Sedan N Monochrome as the lead actor, but one that doesn’t seem to like the spotlight very much. The automaker says it listened to customers who wanted a toned-down and more mature look, and this is what it is giving them now.
Gone is the striking red trim that the standard i30 Sedan N comes with. It has been replaced with body-colored paint for a uniform look. The front bumper inlays, side sills, rear diffuser, and brake calipers are finished entirely in black rather than the usual standout color.
The special edition Hyundai i30 N gains unpainted carbon-fiber mirror caps and a redesigned carbon fiber rear wing spoiler and rides on newly designed 19-inch forged alloy wheels, which are finished in matte black.
Photo: Hyundai Customers can go for one of the two exterior paint options available for the performance sedan: Abyss Black Pearl for a fully blacked-out, murdered-out look, or Performance Blue, which retains the darkened trim pieces.
The Monochrome is the only variant in the entire i30 Sedan N lineup to feature the premium Alcantara-wrapped steering wheel and a matching gear shifter boot. The buttons on the steering wheel have been changed to black to fit the single-tone cockpit. The only color accent on board is the stitching in Performance Blue.
The underpinnings remain identical to the standard model, which means that the car still delivers true track-ready performance. The 2.0-liter turbocharged engine generates 276 horsepower (280 metric horsepower) and 289 pound-feet (392 Newton meters) of torque.
The sedan still rockets from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 4.8 seconds when equipped with the dual-clutch automatic transmission and Launch Control or 5.4 seconds when the six-speed manual transmission is involved.
Photo: Hyundai The all-new Hyundai i30 Sedan N Monochrome will arrive in Australian showrooms starting in November 2026. Only 200 such units will see the light of day with both manual and automatic transmissions.
The official pricing will depend on the market and has yet to be revealed, but it will surely come with a premium over the starting price of the i30 Sedan N standard model, which starts at 53,500 Australian dollars (US $37,316).
Hyundai has plans to launch the performance sedan with restrained looks in Canada, Korea (in late October), and of course, Australia, but its arrival in the United States hasn’t been officially confirmed.

source_document.body:
Northrop Grumman’s new multi-mission radar system has earned effusive praise from Marine Corps leaders as it surges well past the halfway point in fielding. On the heels of that success, officials said this month, other potential customers, including the U.S. Army, have expressed interest in the system.
The AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task Oriented Radar, or G/ATOR, is the Marine Corps’ solution for defending against a broad range of airborne threats , particularly in the Pacific littorals.
It replaces five older radar systems, and last year received an extended-range software upgrade that boosted its capability and advanced its ability to differentiate friends or foes in the air.
In a call with reporters Oct. 7, Northrop Director of Mission Systems Paul Weaver said the company had delivered 43 of the 60 G/ATOR systems the Marine Corps has ordered, of which five are designated for the Air Force and one for Navy test and evaluation.
“Demand for the system in theater right now is high, and it’s based on that performance,” Weaver said. “We’ve been making modifications to the system based on customer input for the last four or five years. We’ve made some hardware modifications that extended its range, and we’re constantly making software improvements to adapt to the specific threat environment, whether that be [unmanned aerial systems], from the smallest to the largest, and other potential threats that they face.”
Weaver said the company was “actively engaged at the headquarters level” with the Marine Corps and the Air Force about how best to employ G/ATOR and had recently begun engagements with the Army as well. While he deferred on saying whether the Army had interest in acquiring the radar system, he said its capabilities had broad appeal across the services.
“When you put a number of these systems in the field, operating in a complementary way, you can stay in constant movement and complicate the adversary’s target cycle,” Weaver said. “That is of interest to every service that’s currently in conflict right now. So, to the level that we’re engaged with the Army and the Air Force, it all comes back to its current performance and the agility that this advanced platform potentially offers.”
At 9,000 pounds, G/ATOR is small and light enough to be transported by C-130 Hercules or MV-22 Osprey aircraft. It can be set up and emplaced by a four-person crew in under ten minutes, and can flex in power settings from 60 kilowatts for medium-range targets to 75 kilowatts for longer-range kills. Initial fielding to the Marine Corps began in 2018, and service leaders have suggested more recently that they might soon expand their acquisition plan.
“We learned that it’s much more capable than we thought,” Brig. Gen. Christopher Haar, now commander of the 3rd Marine Logistics Group, told Military Times last December. “And now there’s a demand for us to get that in more units, and to potentially increase the number of those systems that we buy.”
The War Zone reported last month that the Corps’ Pacific-based 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit had employed the service’s Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) concept for the first time in combat during operations in support of the Operation Epic Fury conflict with Iran. It’s not clear if the G/ATOR system was part of that concept employment. But Weaver did suggest that the current conflict is highlighting its strengths.
With its lightweight footprint and capable 360-degree active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, the system, he said, can be flown into an austere location to establish an expeditionary air base, allowing the establishment of a surveillance perimeter while also enabling airspace control. According to the company, the system can identify launch points of hostile fires ranging from mortars to artillery and serve as a ground-based air traffic control manager. Drone warfare, Weaver said, brings out other strengths.
“It’s proving in recent conflicts and around the globe to perform exceptionally well in clutter, which makes it very helpful in identifying all classes of UASs and cruise missiles,” he said. “It’s not only providing awareness of what’s in the airspace around it at all altitudes. It provides weapons quality data and that performance, which means the warfighter can not only see it but also connect it to any available countermeasure that it has, whether that be kinetic or non-kinetic, and address it appropriately.”

Stellantis Now Builds a Chinese SUV in Europe
19 photos
Photo: Leapmotor
The Leapmotor B10 has joined established B-segment models on the assembly line in Zaragoza, making a move that seemed unrealistic a few short years ago. Stellantis gave a Chinese automaker a European manufacturing base, and this collab should be seen as nothing more than a win-win situation.
Zaragoza in Spain wasn't chosen because Stellantis had a factory available and a big heart. Spare production output played a big role in this decision, and the facility's expertise also counted toward making the Stellantis-Leapmotor partnership a reality. Neither company has disclosed how many B10s the Spanish plant expects to build in the first year of the Euro-centric B10.
Stellantis and Leapmotor , namely a Hangzhou-based automaker founded a little over a decade ago, describe the project as part of a larger effort to make electric mobility that bit more accessible and competitive in Europe. For Leapmotor, of which around 20 percent is owned by Stellantis, the significance of this partnership extends far beyond a compact-sized crossover.
As with any Chinese automaker that has found out how difficult an oversaturated Chinese can be, Europe forms a strategic part of the brand's expansionist ambitions. Producing vehicles in Spain brings Leapmotor closer to the highly lucrative Chinese markets Leapmotor wants to make a name for itself in, while Stellantis gains a larger role in the industrial side of its relationship with the Chinese outfit.
Speaking of all things industrial, the B10's addition to Zaragoza shows how Stellantis can use existing manufacturing operations to accommodate a partner's vehicle. A completely different vehicle, that is, based on a different platform from the CMP of Zaragoza's current products. As of October 2026, those Stellantis-developed models are the Peugeot 208, Opel Corsa, and Lancia Ypsilon.
Photo: Leapmotor Despite this partnership, Leapmotor remains responsible for its own product development and technologies while Stellantis contributes its industrial capabilities and insider knowledge of European markets. The B10's production launch in Spain drew senior political and industrial representatives, with their presence underlining the project's significance for European manufacturing.
The B10 is presently marketed as one of the marque's priciest vehicles in Spain, with prices kicking off at 23,900 euros. Highlight figures include up to 900 kilometers (just under 600 miles) of WLTP driving range for the extended-range setup, 19 minutes from 30 to 80 percent state of charge for the full-electric models, a 14.6-inch central touchscreen, and up to 12 speakers.
Customers in the market for the B10 EV are presented with either 361 or 434 kilometers of range on a full charge, specifically 224 to 270 miles from 56.2 or 67.1 kilowatt -hours. The B10 EREV downgrades to 18.8 kilowatt-hours, but its 50-liter fuel tank more than makes up for it. Being an extended-range electric vehicle, its 1.5-liter internal combustion engine does not drive the wheels. Instead, the engine is tasked with generating electricity whenever needed.
Highlights further include 64-color ambient lighting, 17 driver-assistance functions, an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, NFC key card access, over-the-air software update capability, and LED exterior lights. Last but certainly not least, B10 EV customers get 25 liters of additional storage capacity from the front storage compartment.

Tiny House Florence: An Eco-Friendly Haven Filled with Charming Details
11 photos
Photo: Tiny and Projet Bois
In a world where the costs of living are constantly increasing and the housing crisis seems to spread its tentacles wider, it’s truly comforting to see that tiny homes can be the answers that change some people’s lives for the better. A bespoke tiny house is perhaps a once-in-a-lifetime chance to live in one’s dream house without financial burdens and in perfect harmony with the environment – what could be better?
A tiny house can be many things for its owner, from a cozy vacation home to a full-time residence or a private workshop, but it can also be an all-in-one haven where the owner can live, work, and play in total harmony. Tiny house Florence is an example of that. Named after the woman who became its owner, this wooden cabin on wheels was tailor-made to fit Florence’s specific profession and lifestyle.
It may look plain and traditional on the outside, but this mobile home hides several perks. It incorporates a bespoke sewing area (which makes it unique from the start) and several off-grid and eco-friendly features that raise its sustainability factor considerably, even though this is not a fully self-sufficient home. Last but not least, a few well-chosen style accents take its aesthetic from simple to memorable without a flashy approach.
The story begins with Florence’s 30th birthday. That is when she decided to change her life and become officially a nomad homeowner. Turning 30 is a great time to start living in one’s dream home, but that’s often impossible in terms of conventional housing. For Florence, the option of a tiny home in the beautiful land of Savoy was perfect – it meant full independence, living closer to nature and in harmony with it, and being able to work from home as she pleased.
Photo: Tiny and Projet Bois Both a social worker and a passionate seamstress, Florence wanted her new home on wheels to include a dedicated area for her sewing skills. She was also very lucky to have not just one, but several local farms literally offer to house her new tiny home on their property, free of charge, simply because of her personality and inspirational lifestyle. All she had to do was choose, and she chose a little spot between Chambéry and Albertville for her new tiny home.
With such an auspicious start, tiny house Florence had everything on its side to become a tourist attraction in its own right. Like almost every tiny house built in France, it exudes the timeless charm of a wooden chalet meant for idyllic living. Jean-Maxime, the man who founded Tiny and Projet Bois more than a decade ago, built the perfect layout for Florence and also crafted the small details that make a big difference when it comes to style.
Boasting a little over 23 square feet (7.2 meters) of floor space, tiny house Florence opens the doors to a spacious configuration for one. The only loft serves as the main bedroom (which could easily be a two-person bedroom), and the open-plan ground floor features a charming, cozy lounge at one end, the bathroom at the other end, and the kitchen plus the multi-purpose sewing area in the center.
All of that is wrapped in the natural warmth of the timber paneling throughout, a common feature of almost all tiny homes built in France, and especially for a brand like Tiny and Projet Bois (“Wood Projects”), which offers a wide range of natural wood interior and exterior arrangements, from staircases and furniture to all kinds of terraces, pergolas, and decks.
Photo: Tiny and Projet Bois Jean-Maxime went from engineering to traditional carpentry out of sheer love for wood and a passion for eco-friendly solutions. A true wood wizard, he is both the builder and the main craftsman behind each of the custom tiny homes at Tiny and Projet Bois.
The home’s rear wall reveals a beautiful decorative pattern carved into the wood, which adorns the wall from top to bottom – an unexpected decorative touch that evokes the traditional art of woodcarving, and is also a tribute to Florence’s seamstress profession. Inside, the loft bedroom shows off a beautiful floor-to-ceiling safety wall with an intricate openwork design – another expression of bespoke woodwork and experienced craftsmanship.
Florence’s little sewing corner is actually a versatile area in the center of the house. Built-in wood shelves provide easy-to-reach storage, with a narrow top acting as a small console. A fold-out table with a single leg for stability is primarily meant as the sewing table, but it’s also a great option for serving dinner or for other types of office work. It’s a sewing table, a dinner table, and an office desk, all at once, and it’s perfectly placed to accommodate two to three seats.
Another feature worth noting is the carefully crafted loft staircase with massive built-in storage. This flexible piece of furniture acts both as a wardrobe and a kitchen pantry. Its sturdy cupboards have solid doors, and the wardrobe section features wide, spacious open shelves, plus space for hanging clothes. The tops of these cabinets double as wide treads that connect the loft with the ground floor – it’s a sturdy, reliable staircase that makes accessing the bedroom much safer.
Photo: Tiny and Projet Bois The kitchen cabinetry in itself is compact, but that makes room for a full-size oven to sit right next to it, as well as a dedicated area for the wood-burning stove. This rustic-style stove is part of the home’s range of eco-friendly amenities, and the nook that was dedicated to it includes a wooden stand with storage underneath, and fireproof wall paneling made of removable tiles.
The kitchen cupboards also hide another eco-friendly amenity that is quite rare and unusual – it’s the modern version of a traditional “desert fridge”, originally made from clay. The main thing about this type of fridge is that it doesn’t use any electricity, just evaporative cooling, to keep food cool, and the main disadvantage is the small size. In Florence’s home, it sits hidden inside a dedicated cupboard with ventilation.
This little sustainable home also includes an eco-friendly toilet model, and a rainwater harvesting system – both amenities usually featured in fully off-grid tiny homes. Plus, the house was fitted with removable roof-overhang covers as a natural, low-maintenance way to protect the exterior timber cladding from the elements.
Led lighting and minimalist-style light fixtures throughout complement the home’s simple but cozy aesthetic, while abundant natural light reaches inside through the wide windows and the modern, glazed entrance. The main bedroom itself is a smart combination of privacy and openness, featuring windows on each side of the bed, and a safety railing that, although floor-to-ceiling tall, doesn’t block the view completely.
Photo: Tiny and Projet Bois There’s no formal separation between the lounge and the flexible sewing area, which turns this entire space into a lovely little oasis where Florence can work, relax, welcome guests, and admire the view. A large panoramic window brings the natural surroundings in, and also visually extends the lounge space outside, for an even closer connection to nature.
Compact but crafted with attention to detail, this French tiny home blends functionality with personal touches in a way that makes it unique. From a smart layout that ensures long-term comfort to sustainable amenities, including a rare “desert fridge”, tiny house Florence is perfectly fit for its owner and universally appealing at the same time.

This Camper Is Built on the Back of One of the Most Compact Vehicles in History: A BMW Isetta
16 photos
Photo: yourrandompao | YouTube Screenshot
Campers come in all shapes, sizes, and abilities, and today, we dive into a custom job that is on the compact side of things as much as possible. I mean, it’s built out of a friggin Isetta, one of the quirkiest vehicles the industry has ever created.
Folks, some people may not know that BMW basically pulled themselves away from the brink of bankruptcy with a vehicle dubbed the Isetta . It stood and still stands apart from other vehicles on the market with a design that strips away all side doors, can carry just two people, and was marked by a front end that was the actual door.
To enter the Isetta, we open up the front section of the car, along with the steering mechanism, and climb inside. Primarily, it was this feature that placed the vehicle in the history books.Heck, in the seven years this thing was manufactured, BMW spat out over 161K pieces.
Photo: BMW These days, the Isetta is no longer in production, but recent trends have seen an Isetta-like ride come out of Europe. It’s called the Microlino, and this modern EV continues the “Look at me” effect of the timeless design.
All that brings us to the custom RV before us today, a trinket spotted at Beatersville 2025 car and bike show and posted online by username yourrandompao on YouTube, the very source of all and the only info we have on this Isetta camper.
As we can see, a more traditional and classic Isetta design is used here, with no Microlino features whatsoever showing their teeth, except for the iconic front door, that is. The aluminum handle signals that the base model is clearly an older one.
From there, the entire rear end has been torn off and replaced with a cab-over “stick and tin” construction, as it’s called, and this section of the camper is completed with another door for entry, albeit, a very compact one. By the looks of it, I'd need to turn to the side to wiggle my way into this one, so thank god for the front door.
Photo: yourrandompao | YouTube Screenshot Judging by the clip below, it’s also the most commonly used way to access the interior, with even the owner moving about the cabin via this feature.
What I do want to mention is that it’s clear that the chassis of the Isetta has seen some strong modifications necessary to support the extension on the rear. I think it’s pretty funny that, as we’re driving down the road and seeing this in your rear-view mirror, will be completely different than seeing it pull alongside at a stoplight.
In the video, we can also see the two configurations that are available to this custom job, and yes, by the looks of things, this one can be driven! Pretty wild if you ask me, considering the added weight on the rear of the Isetta and given that the older two-person models could only spit out a peak of 13 hp and rock a displacement of around 300 cc.
In its drive mode, I could make out that there’s only room inside for one person. Most of the left side of the Isetta is occupied with a section that eventually completes the bed, with only the right side of the car offering a seat and access to the steering wheel and pedals. It also appears as though the interior doesn’t need to be converted for a quick nap, with ample bed space available at the rear, even in drive mode.
Photo: yourrandompao | YouTube Screenshot In sleeping or camping mode, the entire interior can be converted into a bed, and it may just be more than enough for two guests to lay their heads down at night.
What I noticed about the rear section of the camper is that it’s covered with a soft top, and while it is screwed in place, I like to entertain the idea that this feature can be taken. Down on sunny days and star-filled nights at campsites or wherever it is you make it with this bite-sized vehicle.
Last but not least, I do want to point out that the Isetta was built with pressed steel panels making up the body, and what I can see in the video below is a body that is completed from a different material, fiberglass, by the looks of it.
If you look closely at the ceiling of the cabin, we can see a smooth transition leading into the cab-over section of the camper, and this leads me to believe that this “Isetta” camper is not actually built out of an actual Isetta, but rather, crafted in the image of one.
Photo: yourrandompao | YouTube Screenshot It’s possible that this applies only to the body as the steering construction when the RV is in drive mode is in the right place and the front and only door is in place where it needs to be, along with the proper open and close action.
The walk-around also reveals that we’re looking at a three-wheeling RV, with just one rear wheel and two at the front. That’s got to be one interesting ride at high speed, if you ask me; it doesn’t look like the most aerodynamic of campers, that’s for sure. A real three-wheel model of the Isetta did see production in the past. The more you know.

Disc Medicine’s bitopertin—rejected by the FDA in February—significantly reduced levels of a key disease biomarker and significantly increased the time patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria were able to spend in the sun and artificial light.
Disc Medicine’s bitopertin helped patients with a rare blood disorder that causes painful sensitivity to the sun spend more time in the light during a pivotal trial, setting the drug up for another attempt at an FDA approval after an accelerated application was rejected last year .
When the results were unblinded “a few days ago,” Disc CEO John Quisel was “overjoyed, as was our whole team,” he told BioSpace in an interview. “Just thrilled to be able to deliver a set of clean results in a set of endpoints that can be tricky.” The results, announced on Monday, revealed that the Phase 3 APOLLO trial hit all primary and secondary endpoints.
Prior to the results, analysts from BMO Capital Markets were optimistic that the readout could clear the way for a regulatory approval in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP). Senior Biopharma Analyst Evan Seigerman told BioSpace that the firm believed there was a high probability that APOLLO would deliver.
Seigerman said bitopertin’s established ability to lower PPIX and the APOLLO trial’s sunlight-exposure endpoint could give Disc a clear path back to regulators. Pivotal rare disease trials are designed to show clear clinical benefit, Seigerman explained. “If that trial hits, then there’s a real path forward for approval.”
The regulatory road for bitopertin to this point has been tricky. In its complete response letter (CRL), revealed in a February 13 SEC filing by Disc, the FDA questioned the biotech’s use of a surrogate endpoint—percent change in whole-blood metal-free protoporphyrin IX (PPIX), the toxic metabolite that drives the disease—as a reasonable predictor of clinical benefit in EPP.
“The percent change in PPIX was relatively modest,” the agency wrote in the CRL, noting that it is unknown whether such magnitude of biomarker effect “is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit.”
Bitopertin was one of the first recipients of the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher in October 2025, granted to products that align with certain national priorities, such as meeting a large unmet medical need or boosting domestic manufacturing. A CNPV entitles the product to a drastically shortened review period of one to two months, down from the typical 10–12 months—but it does not guarantee approval.
In June, Disc announced it had reached an agreement with the FDA whereby the regulator would allow the use of the ongoing APOLLO trial, if successful, to support another regulatory filing for bitopertin. With the new data in hand, Disc plans to resubmit its application—this time for traditional approval of bitopertin—to the FDA by end of the year.

Bitopertin soars in Phase 3
The APOLLO trial, which enrolled 183 adults and adolescents with EPP, showed that bitopertin reduced PPIX by 41.4% compared to placebo (p-value < 0.0001) and increased time patients were able to spend in the light by 12.2 hours during month six (p-value = 0.0010), meeting the study’s two co-primary endpoints with what Quisel called a “high” degree of statistical significance.
All secondary endpoints were also positive, Disc said, including a statistically significant reduction in phototoxic reactions—which Quisel described as “horrifically painful” attacks where the skin is damaged—and increased light tolerance. Exploratory measures of quality-of-life improvement were also statistically significant.
As to the pain attacks, Quisel elaborated on the experience patients have relayed to Disc. “What patients tell us is it feels like they’re being burned or cooked from the inside, because this chemical, PPIX, is floating around in their blood, and when it’s activated by the light, it literally is burning them from the inside.” Many patients receive opioids, even though they don’t address the pain effectively, he added.
Bitopertin was generally well-tolerated with no new safety signals observed in APOLLO, according to Disc’s press release. Dizziness was the most common treatment-emergent adverse event, with 50% of patients in the treatment group experiencing this side effect, but the cases were mild to moderate and generally transient, the company said.
In addition, there were no study discontinuations in the bitopertin arm of the study, “which is remarkable for a six-month study,” Quisel said.
Collectively, the results will support a fresh new drug application for bitopertin. When that filing reaches the FDA, it will face a regulator that looks quite different than it did in February. Former Commissioner Marty Makary, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) director Vinay Prasad and Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) Acting Director Tracy Beth Høeg have all departed the agency. Prasad reportedly intervened in the initial review of bitopertin, expressing his skepticism about the drug’s efficacy.
If Disc’s drug is cleared for the market, it will join Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals’ Scenesse, a subcutaneous implant that is the only treatment approved for EPP and to prevent phototoxic reactions.
Disc began development of bitopertin in 2021 when the company gained global rights to the asset from Roche. At the time, Disc paid an undisclosed upfront fee for the candidate and offered Roche more than $200 million in potential milestone payments.
Still to come
Beyond bitopertin, BMO is bullish on Disc because of the company’s two other clinical assets.
One of those is a monoclonal antibody called DISC-3405, designed to increase the production of hepcidin—a key regulator of iron entry into circulation—to therapeutically reduce iron levels. The drug, licensed from Mabwell Therapeutics in 2023, is being studied in a Phase 2 trial for polycythemia vera (PV) and a Phase 1b study for sickle cell disease.
In early September, Disc said that DISC-3405 increased hepcidin and lowered serum iron in patients with PV, translating to reduced blood draws and symptom burden, according to a poster presentation at the 2026 Society of Hematologic Oncology meeting.

Additional data from RALLY-MF are slated to read out sometime this quarter and are expected to “further clarify the asset’s differentiated profile in myelofibrosis anemia, with end of Phase 2 discussions with FDA providing more details on future Ph 3 trial design,” according to a September report from BMO.
As for bitopertin, Disc said in its press release that an FDA decision is expected by mid-2027. You wouldn’t say that based on the level of new model introductions from ultra-luxury brands like Mercedes-AMG, Ferrari, or Bentley, to name just a few, but it turns out that 2026 hasn’t been the greatest in terms of luxury demand.
However, the likes of Mercedes- AMG with the GT 4-Door Coupe and the new GT SUV , Ferrari with the Luce, Bentley with the new Torcal, or the reinvented Jaguar with the Type 01, among others, continue to churn out one ultra-luxury high-performance model after another. So, why not Lexus too?
The Japanese automaker Toyota’s luxury division saw record sales back in 2025 when it delivered around 882k units globally, but its global and regional sales have taken a negative turn this year due to the perceived overall slowdown in global luxury demand. Also, it’s killing off the LS flagship sedan model in North America as it relies heavily on the crossover and SUV models, leaving only the refreshed IS and the all-new ES to keep the banner up across the passenger car sector.
Well, there are even rumors that the big LS might bite the dust everywhere, not just North America – and some folks don’t like that, including a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI. More precisely, this virtual artist, better known as " Theottle " on social media, says “the end of the Lexus LS marks the conclusion of an extraordinary 36-year legacy.”
The Lexus brand launched back in 1989 with the LS, as any fan of the brand will tell you, and for the author, “with production of Lexus' flagship luxury sedan reportedly ending after the 2026 model year and no direct sedan successor in sight, it's hard not to feel a sense of loss. To me, the LS is the single most important vehicle in Lexus history. It was the model that launched the brand and established its reputation for luxury, refinement, and engineering excellence. Simply put, without the LS, there would be no Lexus.”
No worries, as he’s got a solution; in his latest behind-the-scenes making-of video, he’s ready to continue the legacy beyond 2026. For starters, the author reminds us that the “LS name lives on through three concepts revealed in 2025: the LS Concept people carrier, LS Coupe Concept crossover, and LS Micro Concept box-on-wheels. Of the three, the LS Coupe Concept captured my imagination the most.”
So, he started thinking: “What if Lexus used the LS Coupe Concept as the foundation for an all-new flagship sedan? What would a modern interpretation of the LS look like?” This is the result after some CGI tampering with the sleek crossover SUV. Now it’s a not-so-classic four-door fastback sedan, a setup that is increasingly popular among automakers when it comes to ultra-luxury high-end models like the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, Ferrari Luce, or the new Jaguar Type 01.

This Park Tiny Promises Comfortable Living With Extra-Wide Layout, Private Bedroom, and Large Porch
21 photos
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins
Tiny home design has evolved so much over the last couple of decades, and compact houses are now more diverse and advanced than ever. Not only is the tiny house market offering options to suit every taste, budget, and need, but it also proves that you don’t have to renounce high-end amenities and beautiful aesthetics to live tiny.
Tiny houses like the Wildflower model presented here demonstrate that downsizing doesn't necessarily mean sacrificing comfort or choosing an overly minimalist lifestyle. Built by Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins in Chesnee, South Carolina, the Wildflower is a park model tiny home with generous dimensions that allow for a familiar, easy-to-navigate floor plan, farmhouse-inspired finishes, and a large porch that makes it look like a conventional home.
Run by people passionate about the minimalist and sustainable living movement, Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins has been building stylish, functional park model tiny houses since 2021. Their models are built to the highest standards using premium materials and construction methods typically used in luxury custom homes, blurring the line between traditional houses and mobile dwellings.
Based on a multi-axle trailer, the Wildflower has a length of 41 feet (12.5 meters), which makes it considerably larger than a typical tiny house on wheels. It is also 13.7 feet (4.1 meters) wide, meaning it’s not the kind of home you can easily tow from place to place. Transporting it on public roads requires special permits and towing equipment, so it would be better suited for buyers who plan to keep it in one location or relocate it only occasionally.
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins That extra length and width, however, make a world of difference in how spacious the interior feels, especially considering this is a tiny home for couples. Instead of trying to squeeze in multiple sleeping spaces, the Wildflower is designed with a spacious living area and a private bedroom, offering a tiny home without the cramped feeling often associated with downsizing.
When it comes to exterior finishes, the builder offers customers multiple options to choose from, but the unit featured in the photo gallery is finished in cream and brown engineered wood and a metal roof. Numerous windows all around bring natural light inside and create that coveted connection to nature.
The feature that adds significant curb appeal to the home’s exterior is the large front porch. With a gable roof, composite Trex decking, thick wooden posts, and a black metal railing, it gives the Wildflower a modern-cabin feel and extends the living space to the outside, providing a front-row seat to the surrounding views. It’s large enough to be fitted with patio furniture and looks like a really nice place to enjoy a cuppa or host guests.
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins This park model tiny ’s interior reveals why dimensions matter so much when it comes to making small-space living comfortable. With 400 square feet (37 square meters) of living space and a cleverly configured floor plan, it proves small living can still feel open, comfortable, and refined.
Laid out on a single level, it includes a welcoming lounge, a well-equipped kitchen, a full bathroom, and a private ground-floor bedroom. And then, there are the little details that make it a great fit for full-time occupancy: the full-size appliances, a stacked washer/dryer, a built-in dedicated closet for clothes, a fireplace, a large pantry, air conditioning, and more.
Style-wise, the entire living space combines warm, rustic elements with contemporary finishes. Light whitewashed pine shiplap walls, a natural wood plank ceiling, and warm timber accents are paired with light sage-green cabinetry, black hardware, and soft textiles to create a calm, comfortable atmosphere.
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins As you step inside, the lounge is open and welcoming, with space for multiple seating options, like a full sofa and a couple of armchairs. It is rich in natural light due to multiple large windows and a full-light glass door that looks out onto the deck area. The front wall serves as the room’s focal point, featuring warm-toned vertical wood planks, a built-in electric fireplace, and a decorative mantel shelf.
The lounge flows into a modern cottage-style kitchen with sage-green cabinetry and white solid-surface countertops. The space is efficiently arranged to ensure maximum functionality , with plenty of storage, a full-height pantry, and a separate cabinet that can double as a coffee station. And thanks to the L-shape of the countertop, there is a kitchen island overhang with two modern dark brown leather barstools tucked underneath.
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins A comprehensive suite of stainless-steel appliances make this kitchen feel residential and function accordingly. It is equipped with a gas range, an over-the-range microwave, a double-door fridge, and an under-counter dishwasher, with a double-bowl sink completing the package.
Behind the pantry and coffee station, we find the bathroom. It is not very large, but includes all the essentials for full-time living. The 60-inch one-piece shower stall comes with a built-in seat, while the vanity features an elongated counter and ample storage underneath. There is also a wall-mounted linen closet and enough room to move around comfortably.
Photo: Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins As mentioned, this is a park tiny RV aimed at couples who love space and comfort, so there is only one bedroom in this model. It’s positioned at the rear and is completely private. It accommodates a queen bed flanked by 16-inch nightstands and includes a large wardrobe with shelving and hanging space. There’s also space to walk around the bed, and the room also integrates a stacked washer and dryer for added convenience.
For those looking for a compact home with an appealing cabin look, a private ground-floor bedroom, and room to enjoy life both indoors and out, the Wildflower park model tiny home might be a great fit. Sweet-Haus Tiny Cabins offers this model for $115,000.

In the wake of a successful IPO and strong stock growth throughout the year, Veradermics now has late-stage data to support a regulatory package for its hair loss pill.
Coming off a February IPO that brought in more than $256 million, hair loss biotech Veradermics’ lead asset has shown improved hair coverage in men during a Phase 3 trial.
VDPHL01, which is an oral extended-release formulation of minoxidil, which showed significant improvement in patient-reported outcomes over placebo.
The clinical results cap off a meteoric year for the biotech since the IPO, which was followed by a massive stock surge in the ensuing months. The Connecticut-based drugmaker had been building up to the release of late-stage data for the drug candidate, called VDPHL01, which sets the company up for potential FDA approval.
The trial, named Study 304, included more than 500 males with mild-to-moderate pattern hair loss who received either VDPHL01 once or twice a day, or placebo. For one of the two co-primary endpoints measuring hair thickness, patients in the once-daily group had an improvement of 28.6 hairs per square centimeter, while the twice-daily cohort saw an improvement of 36.4 hairs per square centimeter, compared with 6.6 hairs per square centimeter for placebo comparators after six months.

After debuting on the public markets with $256.3 million and raking in an additional $472 million , Veradermics has emerged as one of biotech’s biggest post-IPO standouts. CEO Reid Waldman credits the weight loss craze for establishing consumer-driven channels.

On the second endpoint that measured patient-reported outcomes, 55.7% of men in the once-daily cohort showed “improved” or “much improved” hair coverage based on a rating of alopecia severity, while 68.7% in the subset that received twice-daily medication reported the same. Of patients in the placebo group, 15% reported improvement.
A secondary measure of investigator perception of hair growth was also statistically significant, with 78.8% of once-daily patients and 82.7% of twice-daily patients showing improvement, compared to 35.3% of patients in the placebo group.
Veradermics designed its version of minoxidil, also the main ingredient in the household hair loss brand Rogaine, to be delivered in an extended-release formulation using a gel matrix for sustained absorption to improve efficacy and safety, according to the company. The delivery method helps avoid high peak concentrations, allowing more time for hair growth, the company said in a release.
For the approximately 50 million men and 30 million women with pattern hair loss, also called androgenetic alopecia, no FDA-approved treatment has entered the U.S. market in almost 30 years, according to Veradermics.
The company has not announced a timeline for a regulatory submission but said the data would be used to support an application. The company plans to hold a conference call Monday morning to discuss the results.
Veradermics CEO Reid Waldman told BioSpace in July that the thriving consumer market behind GLP-1 weight loss drugs from industry giants Eli Lilly and Novo helped convince him and his team that “hair loss could be the next weight loss,” demonstrating that patients would be willing to take certain parts of healthcare into their own hands.
In addition to Study 304, Veradermics is running an ongoing Phase 2/3 trial called Study 302 featuring men with pattern hair loss. This study has already shown similar efficacy results and will contribute to the future regulatory submission. Updated results from a second part of Study 302 will be revealed later this year, according to the company.
The small drugmaker has also finished enrollment in a Phase 2/3 study for female pattern hair loss and expects to read out results in the first half of next year.
Veradermics is not the only biotech in the game. Pelage Pharmaceuticals is also racing to market with a novel therapy called PP405 that is currently in Phase 2/3 testing. A Phase 2a read out last year showed that 31% of male patients with a higher degree of hair loss had a greater than 20% increase in hair density at week eight.

Old-School Google Maps Rival Now Lets You Track Flock Cameras on the Map
9 photos
Photo: MapQuest
You’re not old if you've never heard of MapQuest. But no matter your age, the navigation software that has been around since 1996 has just offered everybody a very, very, very good reason to install its mobile app.
It all comes down to these two words: Flock cameras.
MapQuest has just added a new Surveillance Layer that allows users to see nearby Flock cameras and other surveillance systems directly on the map. If you’ve been concerned about your privacy and followed all the controversy around Flock cameras, you probably know that user communities out there have been working on ways to make these surveillance systems easier to track .
But no big company has ever released such a feature. MapQuest is the first to do so, adding support for automatic license plate readers, also known as APLRs, and public cameras from many other companies, including Flock, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, and Verkada.
If you wonder why MapQuest has decided to embrace such an approach at a time when nobody seems to be exploring such an update - for example, neither Google Maps nor Apple Maps offer the possibility to see Flock cameras on the map - it’s because the company has turned these user-oriented updates into its modus operandi.
MapQuest has recently made the headlines after refusing to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, whereas all the other big mapping platforms honored President Donald Trump’s executive order.
MapQuest announced the update in a post titled “the roads have eyes,” revealing that the brand-new Surveillance Layer is available for all users in the Map Options section of its mobile app. Once enabled, you can see nearby Flock cameras. If you zoom out, you’ll see all surveillance systems in your region, along with the direction where they are oriented.
The application doesn’t yet offer an option to set up a route that avoids Flock cameras, and it’s unclear if such a feature is currently on the radar.
Flock cameras have been facing intense criticism from users and privacy advocates, who warned that in addition to license plates, these surveillance cameras can also log information like vehicle details, direction, and timestamps. The data, these critics claim, allows an individual to be tracked without a warrant.
While Flock said that its cameras make the US safer, the public backlash has evolved into people vandalizing the surveillance systems in multiple regions.
If you want to see Flock cameras on the map, make sure you are running the latest MapQuest app version (Android or iOS). After the update, tap the layers icon in the bottom right corner of the screen in the map view and click the toggle next to Surveillance. When you return to the map view, you should now see Flock cameras on the map with an eye icon. Originally Built for a Billionaire Heiress, This Rare Yacht Now Sports a Modest Price Tag
26 photos
Photo: IYC
Although not remarkably innovative in terms of engineering or interior design, this 40-meter (131 feet) yacht is special in more ways than one. It’s one of the very few Kiwi-built luxury yachts, for a short while it bore the name of a great Canadian personality, and it eventually became a rare catch as the original shipyard that had delivered it in 2009 ceased operations.
When you’re a billionaire and the heiress of an enduring media empire, you can have your pick of luxury pleasure craft. Most people in this situation choose ultra-sophisticated, behemoth-sized, and even futuristic megayachts built by the world’s top names in the superyacht industry, such as the greatest Dutch, German, or Italian shipyards. The late Loretta Ann Rogers, who passed away in 2022, went a very different route.
There were four yachts that bore her name, and all came from the same shipyard - a relatively young builder in New Zealand, with an unusual history, and sadly a short career, eventually ceasing operations in 2016. That choice is highly unusual for someone with the wealth and status of the Rogers heiress, and it makes all of these four yachts rare and special. Delivered in 2009, Vesper is the one that flaunted this name for a short while, but it’s no less unique than the others.
The fact that Loretta Ann Rogers chose to commission these pleasure craft throughout the years indicates her close bond, described as a patronage type of relationship, with the New Zealand-based shipyard, and it certainly leaves a considerable heritage behind for this brand. AY28, and then AY32 were the first two official Loretta Ann yachts. AY32, launched in 2005, was named Ab Initio, and the AY38 (currently Vesper) that would be launched in 2009 was based on it.
Photo: IYC According to the builder himself, AY38 was only a placeholder while the bigger AY43 was under construction. That is why AY38, launched as Allogante, quickly changed its name to Loretta Ann IV, but then “transferred” this name to the AY43, once that was completed and delivered. The AY43 (most recently known as Ab Initio) was, at 47 meters (154 feet) the largest Alloy Yachts build.
The builder referred to the Rogers heiress as “a noted philanthropist, talented artist, environmentalist and compassionate superyacht owner” and indicated that this final yacht, the AY43, also reflected “the culmination of years of ownership experience”.
Loretta Ann and her four children had all inherited a large stake in Roger Communications, after Ted Rogers passed away in 2008. This telecoms and media empire provides cable TV, telephone, and internet services, and it also owns Canada's largest publisher, Rogers Publishing.
Early on, the Rogers family was also recognized for its philanthropy. In 2014, the Rogers $130 million donation to establish the Ted Rogers Centre for Heart Research became the largest single donation in the history of Canadian health care. Loretta also founded the Loretta A. Rogers Chair in Eating Disorders at Toronto General & Western Hospital.
Photo: IYC Originally named Allogante, Vesper was launched in 2009. At the time, it was described as a development of the 2005 Ad Lib (another one of the Loretta Ann yachts mentioned prior), incorporating all of its signature features, but also boasting the best technical upgrades available. Like most luxury motor yachts by Alloy Yachts, it was the result of a collaboration between Dubois Naval Architects and Donald Starkey (for the interior design).
After its 2009 debut, this 40-meter yacht changed hands quite a few times. The original launch name was Allogante, then it was named Loretta Ann while it served as a placeholder for her bigger yacht. Over the years, it was also known as Tat’s, So Nice, and is currently back on the market as Vesper.
Although not necessarily innovative or outstanding in terms of style, Vesper is remarkable for its size category. That’s mainly because it offers an unusual amount of outdoor space, similar to a much bigger yacht. Plus, it offers the benefit of a shallow draft (2.3 meters/7.5 feet) that allows it to access bays that are forbidden for yachts of the same length, but larger.
This was an important requirement for the late heiress, as the larger Loretta Ann (47 meters) also had a shallow draft specifically for easy access to the Bahamas and Belize.
Photo: IYC All Alloy Yachts motor yacht share the distinctive deep navy blue hull color that makes them easily recognizable, along with a modern, angular silhouette that hints at a sporty performance. Vesper flaunts the same signature look, and its smart, flexible layout can be described as a heaven for extended vacations on the water. Its unusually large sun deck is basically an entire floor of the yacht that offers a jacuzzi, a bar, shaded al-fresco dining and BBQ, all on one level.
The jacuzzi is placed aft, surrounded by sun loungers and in proximity to a full bar. The barbecue station added here means that the crew don’t have to waste time moving between the galley and the sun deck, since everything can be prepared right there, on deck. The foredeck reveals another sun lounging area, with an unusual hammock swing (rigged off the side deck) added for relaxation.
The main deck aft is also somewhat unusual because of its high flexibility. It was purposely designed to switch easily between a dining setup with a generously-sized table for lunch, and a cocktail setup with a low coffee table and cozy sofas all around. In addition to that, the classic dining area is easily accessed from the salon on the main deck, and it even comes with a full-stocked wine gallery.
In terms of accommodation, a total of five cabins can welcome up to 12 guests, plus separate quarters for a crew of seven. The master suite enjoys the best placement (forward on the main deck) and it has enough floor space for a separate study and a walk-in wardrobe. All the other four cabins are on the lower deck, and they include a twin cabin with Pullman berths for added flexibility.
Photo: IYC The side-opening tender garage, which doubles as a water-level gym, houses a big (16.6 feet) Williams Dieseljet tender and dive compressor. Two more personal watercraft (PWCs) are stored on the foredeck, and can be handled using the dedicated deck crane.
Built to Lloyd’s classification and constantly well-maintained, Vesper enjoyed a successful charter career over the years, with weekly rates in the Mediterranean starting at €126,000. It was most recently refitted in Spain in 2025, and is currently asking for €10,9 million ($12.2 million).
Vesper is not only one of the few yachts that were owned and named after one of the greatest contemporary philanthropists, but also a rare Kiwi yacht. Alloy Yachts, the New Zealand-based builder, brought to life some of the best sailing yachts of the ‘90s, including the 159-foot sloop Georgia, which became the world’s largest single-mast sailing yacht at the time.
Photo: IYC Sadly, because the demand for sailing yachts dropped dramatically, and because of challenging economic times for New Zealand’s exporters, Allow Yachts decided to end its operations in 2016. This means that there is a limited number of Alloy Yachts pleasure craft still out there, and there will never be a new one (at least, not in the foreseeable future). Vesper is a collector’s item for this reason alone, and valuable beyond its $12 million price tag.

Refreshed Honda Accord e:HEV Gets $1,000 Pricier in Australia for 2027
9 photos
Photo: Honda
Priced AUD 1,000 higher than its predecessor, the 2027 Honda Accord e:HEV is barely different from the 2026 model when you analyze their specification sheets side by side. The Japanese automaker has tidied up a few choice exterior details, added some red stitching for good measure, cut the complimentary Honda Connect subscription from 5 to 3 years, and that's pretty much it.
Honda's Aussie subsidiary couldn't make a case for any powertrain updates, and there is no additional standard kit to soften the price increase either, leaving the Accord between a rock and a hard place. The 2027 model does little to give prospective customers a fresh reason to choose it over the Toyota Camry, which is exclusively four-pot hybrid in the Australian market since 2024.
Even its stylistic updates are hard to notice unless you park the 2027 Accord right next to its forerunner. Honda started by replacing the gloss-black lower body trim pieces and headlight surrounds with body-color trim. A black insert now occupies the lower front bumper where silver trim used to sit, and the amber reflectors of the front lighting units have disappeared for a cleaner aesthetic.
Honda further deleted the blue outlines previously used on the exterior badges, yet the e:HEV lettering that designates the hybrid four-cylinder powertrain remains on the trunk lid. Hopping inside, the biggest difference over the 2026 and earlier models is the adoption of red stitching throughout the cabin. The infotainment system and other equipment otherwise carry over.
That means Accord buyers are presented with a 10.2-inch digital instrument cluster, an 11.5-inch HUD, 12.3 inches of central infotainment touchscreen, and 12 audio speakers from Bose. A panoramic sunroof, 360-degree cameras, and cordless Apple CarPlay plus Android Auto remain standard. Heated front seats are notably absent, which is ridiculous when smaller and cheaper vehicles now come with heating in the front seats by default.
Photo: Honda Given the drive-away price of nearly AUD 66,000 before options, that omission is definitely uncomfortable. Honda Australia has essentially increased the starting price without giving the mid-sized sedan a standard feature that would make those additional AUD 1,000 easier to justify against the Camry and similar vehicles.
And that's not all, though, for Honda Australia has nerfed the Honda Connect complimentary subscription by 2 years. The service handles a number of remote functions, including remote locking and unlocking, climate control, location information, and vehicle status. All things considered, the Accord e:HEV is clearly moving in the wrong direction for 2027.
The bad news continues with Honda Australia's low-price scheduled servicing, which now costs AUD 279 per visit instead of AUD 199 prior to October 2026. That increase is separate from the Accord's 2027 facelift , but forms part of the ownership arithmetic for anyone looking at a brand-new Accord today. Under the hood, a familiar 2.0-liter naturally aspirated I4 hybrid soldiers on with 135 kW (181 hp) and 335 Nm (247 lb-ft) on tap.
Per the attached specifications sheet, the front-drive sedan drinks 4.3 liters per 100 kilometers (54.7 miles per gallon US) in the combined test cycle, based on the ADR 81/02 testing procedure. Undoubtedly respectable by mid-size sedan standards, but still 0.3 liters off the Camry, which is hardly a surprise when you remember that Toyota has the more efficient internal combustion engine and hybrid system to boot.

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
19 October 2026
Pressures at the US’s southern border, from rising volumes and diminished trucking capacity, are causing shippers to evaluate transloading.
According to Uber Freight, this is turning from an emergency solution into a structural network element.
Uncertainty about the future of Mexico’s free-trade agreement with the US has not made a dent in the rise of truck border crossings. Trade between the neighbours rose to $94.8bn in July, up 27.5% from a year earlier, and more than 70% of this crosses the border on trucks.
While volume kept growing, capacity has been hit by US enforcement of trucking regulations, notably English language proficiency rules and cabotage restrictions. The pool of B1 drivers, who pick up freight in Mexico and deliver it to the US, has been reduced by 25,000 between April of last year and this month.
The strain has been building: Uber Freight has counted three occasions this year so far when shippers, reliant on B1 drivers, “got stuck with backlogs of 30, 40, sometimes 50 loads, when that capacity wasn’t there”.
All of these blockages occurred at the Laredo crossing, which handles about 40% of US-Mexico commercial traffic. Official numbers of daily crossings at the bottleneck vary between 17,000 and 21,000 trucks a day.
CANACAR, Mexico’s national trucking association, has acknowledged the importance of combating illegal cabotage, but warned of operational challenges for Mexican operators, and additional delays at the border due to increased inspections and documentation requirements that complicate driver scheduling, equipment positioning, and delivery times.
Washington appears unlikely to ease its enforcement drive on the trucking industry. Logistics providers like CH Robinson have warned customers that cross-border capacity could tighten further this quarter.
The driver shortage is not a temporary setback but a structural issue, said Kyle Toombs, SVP of capacity solutions at Uber Freight.
“Some of these drivers may requalify over time, but losing a visa is hard to come back from, and in the meantime that capacity isn’t paused, it’s gone,” he commented.
On top of the driver shortage, rising operating costs, higher interest rates, and tighter lending conditions are discouraging new trucking companies from entering the market.
Now, the disparity between capacity and volume is causing a growing number of cargo owners to look at transloading as a strategic measure to limit the impact of border disruptions and driver shortages, Mr Toombs reported.
Historically the concept has been viewed as a stopgap measure used by smaller shippers, but it is now getting attention from larger firms as well, including industries like automotive and electronics that eschewed transloading.
Mr Toombs said: “A lot of large, middle-market enterprise-type companies are now looking at it.”
And the concept itself is being viewed in a new light, he added.
“Over the past year, transloading has shifted from an emergency workaround into something shippers deliberately design into their networks from day one. It isn’t a reaction to a rough patch. It’s a structural response to a labour pool that isn’t coming back the way it was,” he said.
Transloading serves as a pressure valve to deal with disruptions to cross-border flows, tapping into a larger pool of drivers, but it can be elevated to become a plank in a shipper’s transport strategy.
“If a product can transload, it can also run through trailer. That means transloading isn’t a trade-off against existing through-trailer capacity; it’s incremental volume added on top of it. The shippers getting this right aren’t treating it as either-or. They’re building both capabilities, putting the right controls around the warehouses and cross docks they use to protect product integrity, and making the cost-versus-service call lane by lane. Often, they don’t have to choose at all,” Mr Toombs explained.
According to him, capacity for transloading is “fairly sufficient”, as it does not require much warehouse capacity and there is an ample labour pool available.
The cost differential between transloading and end-do-end trucking fluctuates, but on balance through-trailer cost is “a bit higher”, he said, adding that transloading charge at the border is about $150-$200.
Companies that want to build up a transloading leg should start out by mapping their network lane by lane, tracking the regulatory signals, and building the necessary relationships and warehouse controls, he advised.
“Make sure your customs broker is looped in and that you use C-TPAT-certified carriers,” he added.
In terms of mixing transloading with through-trailer use, Mr Toombs recommended “at least 10-15% of total volume” to the former. “
You can increase this if, and when, you want,” he said.
While most transloading is happening at Laredo, firms are also using other border points like El Paso, and a growing number are using more than one location for transloading, he noted.
